title: Module 3 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A correlation of −.80 is weaker than a correlation of +.40.
items.why: Strength is the absolute value. Negative .80 is stronger than positive .40.

items.s: A correlation of .50 means that 50 percent of the variability is shared.
items.why: You need r squared. .50 squared is .25, so 25 percent of the variability is shared.

items.s: Correlation proves causation if the sample is large enough.
items.why: Sample size changes confidence in the estimate. It does not change the research design.

items.s: r can take a value of 1.35 if the relationship is very strong.
items.why: r is bounded by negative one and positive one. A value outside that range signals a computational error.

items.s: Sample variance divided by n gives a biased estimate of the population variance.
items.why: On average it falls short of the true value, which is why the n minus 1 correction is used.

items.s: A scatterplot should be examined before trusting a correlation.
items.why: Outliers, curves, and restricted ranges can make r misleading.

items.s: Whether you divide by N or n minus 1 when computing variance
items.why: Divide by N if your scores are the whole population. Divide by n minus 1 if you are estimating from a sample, which is the usual case.

items.s: Two variables with r = 0 are unrelated in every way.
items.why: Pearson r only detects linear association. A strong curved relationship can produce r near zero.
